sections.Ask together: In the end the barrier isn't rebuilt by hiding better — it's rebuilt by singing the truth out loud, patterns showing. Why is the TRUE version stronger than the PERFECT version?
sections.For the grown-up: This is the whole repair arc landing at once: rupture (the secret), armor (the hiding), truth (spoken — sung — at last), return (to her friends and the stage), and a restoration that re-equips her: a barrier made of honesty instead of performance, stronger than the original, like Maui's new hook. Closing couch question: what's OUR family's version of singing it instead of hiding it?

items.name: 📚 Appendix — what did not fit: Korean shamanism, minhwa, the knot

metadata.card_subtitle: Sources and public-domain images, for anyone who wants to go further.

sections.Note: Everything below this card is source material, not fan-made videos — it is the research block pulled across from a separate film project (HOT POTATO), where the Korean shamanism behind the movie was being read seriously. It holds documentary and lecture clips about gut (굿) and mudang, two recordings of a real gut performed at a shrine in Seoul, a short quote from the Netflix art book about where the ancient-hunters sequence came from, eighteen public-domain minhwa (Korean folk paintings) from Wikimedia Commons with full museum credit, nine public-domain knot and interlace images for anyone curious about where the HUNTR/X emblem and the Honmoon get their shape, and three openly-licensed recordings of Arirang. None of it fits the watch-together spirit of the playlist above — it is here for anyone who wants to go further.

items.name: Gut · 굿 — what the music actually is

metadata.card_subtitle: A ceremony a community does, and does again.

sections.Note: A Korean ceremony, still performed: the house gods invited in, what harms sent off. Not a battle — something a community does, and does again. The demons are not defeated. The barrier is kept.
sections.Where this text comes from: A title card written for the HOT POTATO film, where it marks the turn from arguing about a problem to carrying a real ceremony underneath the rest of the footage. Reproduced here because it is the shortest honest answer to "what is a gut, and why does the movie sound like that?"

items.name: Where the ancient hunters came from — an artist remembering his mother, a Korean shaman

credit.artist: Won Sul Hyun (visual development artist), quoted by Tracey Miller-Zarneke
credit.source: Printed art book — quoted, not reproduced
credit.edition: The Art of KPop Demon Hunters (Netflix)
credit.license: Copyrighted; one short line quoted with attribution for commentary

metadata.card_subtitle: One line from the Netflix art book, quoted with credit.

sections.Note: The film's opening sequence — the ancient hunters — was drawn by visual development artist Won Sul Hyun from his memories of his mother, a Korean shaman, performing gut. In his own words he was "witnessing her incredibly charismatic and spiritual performances during Gut" — ceremonies, he says, filled with live music and driven by Korean percussion. The fiction and the practice are not neighbours: one is made out of the other.
sections.Source: The Art of KPop Demon Hunters, written by Tracey Miller-Zarneke (Netflix), Chapter 2 — Ancient Hunters. Film directed by Maggie Kang and Chris Appelhans. One line quoted with attribution for commentary; the book's photographs and artwork are not reproduced anywhere in this playlist.
sections.The colours: On the same page, his palette is traced to the sam taegeuk — blue for Sky, red for Earth, yellow for Humanity, the three turning together as one. Character designer Marion Bordeyne worked from Obangsaek, the traditional Korean five colours, weaving armor and hanbok together.

items.name: Tiger and Magpie (Hojakdo) — Joseon period

sections.Why: The classic minhwa joke: a huge, awkwardly-drawn tiger sits under a pine while a small magpie scolds it from a branch. Folklorists read it as low mocking high — the tiger of power looking ridiculous beside the bird that is not afraid of it.

items.name: Tiger and Magpie — 19th-century hanging scroll

sections.Why: The same motif as a tall hanging scroll — the composition reads top to bottom, magpie above, tiger below.

items.name: Tiger door painting, Korean Folk Village — folk-style, wood-printed

credit.artist: Unknown (folk-style, Joseon-period design); photograph released to the public domain by the photographer

sections.Why: The highest-resolution tiger in this set, good for a close crop of the face. Caveat worth keeping: this is a photograph of a wood-printed minhwa on a hanok door at a folk-village museum, not a period antique painting.

items.name: Jar with tiger and magpie designs — porcelain, c. 1700–1800

credit.museum: Asian Art Museum of San Francisco

sections.Why: The same tiger-and-magpie joke in underglaze cobalt on a jar — proof the motif travelled well beyond painting and turns up on the things people actually used.

items.name: Rank badge with a pair of tiger-leopards (hyungbae) — early 19th century

sections.Why: The tiger as official insignia, embroidered onto a rank badge — a different flavour of the same animal: not the folk joke, but the tiger of bureaucratic authority.

items.name: Sipjangsaengdo — ten symbols of longevity, by Chae Yong-shin, 1921

credit.artist: Chae Yong-shin (채용신) — named, unusual for minhwa
credit.museum: Not stated on the file page

sections.Why: Sun, mountains, water, rocks, clouds, pine, the mushroom of immortality, tortoise, crane, deer — ten slow things that last, arranged together on purpose. An extremely wide format, made for reading across rather than at once.

items.name: Sipjangsaengdo folding screen — National Palace Museum, Changdeok 6447

credit.museum: National Palace Museum of Korea, Changdeok collection 6447

sections.Why: The largest and most complete screen in this set — a full multi-panel scan at enormous resolution, with the whole ten-symbol vocabulary present. Also the best example in the appendix of Obangsaek, the five traditional colours, used across a whole surface.

items.name: Jangsaengdo (Longevity) — National Palace Museum, Changdeok 6445

credit.museum: National Palace Museum of Korea, Changdeok collection 6445

sections.Why: A second, distinct painting of the same longevity set from the same collection — useful where the screen above would be a repeat.

items.name: Deer amid pine trees — from the Ten Symbols of Longevity scrolls, 19th century

sections.Why: Two of the ten symbols on their own — deer and pine — in the tighter hanging-scroll format. Where the big screens overwhelm, this one is readable at a glance.

items.name: Bowl decorated with the ten symbols of longevity — 19th century

sections.Why: The longevity symbols on a bowl someone ate from — the same everyday travel of a motif as the tiger jar above.

items.name: Chaekkori — a scholar's bookshelf screen, 19th century

credit.museum: Via the Google Art Project; holding museum not stated on the file page

sections.Why: Chaekgeori screens are inventories of what a cultivated life keeps close — books, brushes, vases, porcelain. Extreme-wide format and very high detail.

items.name: Chaekgeori (Bookshelves) — dated 1800

credit.museum: Not stated on the file page

sections.Why: A cleaner single-panel composition than the wide screens — easier to read if the multi-panel versions are too busy.

items.name: Books and Scholars' Possessions (Chaekgeori) — early 20th century

sections.Why: A later chaekgeori, the genre still going into the twentieth century — the shelves keep filling long after the court stopped commissioning them.

items.name: Irworobongdo — the Sun, Moon and Five Peaks

credit.year: Not stated on the file page; the genre is a standard Joseon court screen type
credit.museum: Not stated on the file page

sections.Why: This screen always stood directly behind the king's throne — literally the backdrop a ruler's authority was measured against. The closest thing in Korean court painting to a cosmic order a figure stands in front of, which is roughly what a Honmoon is in the film.
sections.Heads up: The only genuine painting of this motif that cleared a public-domain licence at usable resolution. Every palace-interior photograph showing the screen in situ is licensed CC-BY-SA and was rejected.

items.name: Munjado — eight-panel screen of pictorial characters

credit.museum: Not stated on the file page

sections.Why: Each panel is a Confucian virtue — filial piety, loyalty, trust, propriety, righteousness, integrity, shame, brotherly love — built out of pictures rather than written as words. The nearest thing in the minhwa canon to a code of values you can hang on a wall.

items.name: Where the knot comes from — family resemblance, not descent

metadata.card_subtitle: Two traditions that never met, arriving at the same shape.

sections.Note: Family resemblance, not descent. The HUNTR/X emblem and the Honmoon draw on Korean maedeup knotting and the Buddhist endless knot, which reached Korea from India. Other interlace traditions — Islamic girih, Celtic knotwork, Roman guilloche — arrived at the same shape separately. There are only so many ways to draw one unbroken line folding back on itself.
sections.Heads up: The maedeup reading of the logo is careful fan and analyst close-reading, not a confirmed studio statement — no on-record quote from the directors or Sony's production design team naming maedeup, dancheong or sam taegeuk as the source was found. This card was written to answer a question about whether the emblem shares a lineage with the woven octagon used in Sufi calligraphic art. It does not: those two traditions never met.

items.name: The endless knot — the Tibetan Buddhist form

credit.artist: Uploader, released to the public domain

sections.Why: One of Buddhism's Eight Auspicious Symbols, traced to Indus Valley seals around 2500 BC and carried across Tibet, Mongolia, China, Japan and Korea with Buddhism itself. Clean line art, no cultural markers, easy to recolour.

items.name: The endless knot — shaded rendering

credit.artist: Uploader, released to the public domain

sections.Why: The same symbol drawn with over-and-under shading, so the single unbroken line is actually legible as one line.

items.name: Eight-pointed star (khatam form)

credit.license: Public domain (simple geometry, ineligible for copyright)

sections.Why: The eight-pointed star that underlies a great deal of Islamic geometric design — the frame that a woven interior usually sits inside.

items.name: Eight-pointed star — construction variants

sections.Why: Several ways of building the same eight-pointed figure side by side — useful for seeing that the shape is a construction, not a drawing.

items.name: Octagon knotwork cross / interlaced octagram

credit.artist: Uploader, released to the public domain

sections.Why: The closest shape in this set to a woven octagon — one line, over and under, inside an eight-sided frame. The form that keeps reappearing in unrelated traditions.

items.name: Interlaced pentagram strapwork

credit.artist: Uploader, released to the public domain

sections.Why: Girih (Persian for knot) is continuous knotted strapwork generated from a small set of polygon tiles, attested in the Islamic world from the 9th–12th centuries — its own deep root is Greco-Roman interlace, a third lineage that never touched Buddhist Asia.

items.name: A Beautiful Woman (Miindo), by Shin Yun-bok — wearing a norigae

sections.Why: The one image in this group that is identifiably Korean and shows an actual knot ornament being worn — a red three-piece norigae, the maedeup knotting tradition the HUNTR/X emblem is read as drawing on. Each of the three leads in the film has her own norigae.
sections.Heads up: Every photograph of real maedeup or norigae on Wikimedia Commons is licensed CC-BY-SA, so none qualified for this public-domain set. This painting stands in for them.

items.name: Arabesque interlace, the Alhambra — Patio de los Leones

sections.Why: Historic Islamic octagonal interlace as actually built — the same logic of one line folding back on itself, five thousand kilometres and an entirely separate lineage away from the endless knot.

items.name: Geometric wall detail, the Alhambra

sections.Why: A second Alhambra detail — the pattern at wall scale rather than in a frame.

items.name: Arirang — Jindo version (open recording)

metadata.card_subtitle: An audio file on Wikimedia Commons — link in Source.

sections.Note: Arirang is the Korean folk song with dozens of regional variants — Jeongseon, Jindo, Miryang, Gyeonggi — inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list by South Korea in 2012 and North Korea in 2014. The refrain, 아리랑 아리랑 아라리요 (Arirang, arirang, arariyo), is closer to a wordless sound of longing than to a sentence: scholars do not agree that "arirang" means anything in particular. It is sung by everyone together after each verse, rather than as a leader-and-room exchange.
sections.Source: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/48/Jindo_Arirang.wav — an audio file, not a video. Commons file page: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jindo_Arirang.wav

items.name: The shamanic songs themselves — why none of them are here

metadata.card_subtitle: A living religion, not folklore free for the taking.

sections.Note: The songs sung inside a gut are called muga, and they are not folk songs — a mudang sings them, in a ceremony, for someone. Bari-degi tells of the abandoned princess who crosses into the underworld and becomes the permanent guide of the dead rather than death's conqueror. Jindo Ssitgim-gut washes a dead person's han away so the soul can pass on, and is performed for every death in the community, again and again. Binari is a blessing that names what threatens before it asks for what is needed. None of these has a verifiably open recording: a search of Wikimedia Commons, the Korean government's open-content portal and the national archives turned up Arirang and instrumental court music, and no ritual muga.
sections.Why the card exists: Korean shamanism (Mugyo) is a living, currently-practised religion with real mudang, not a dead tradition free for the taking. Quoting Arirang is low risk — it is sung by everyone and claimed by no one. Lifting a real mudang's chant out of a real ceremony and looping it as background texture is a different act, and the honest routes are to license a recording properly, to stay with the open Arirang files above, or to borrow the shape of a practice rather than its sung content.

description: Great KPop Demon Hunters video worth watching together, in one place: dance covers from crews around the world, prop and costume builds to try at home, fan films and musician covers, the real Korean hair, dress and legends behind the movie, a seven-question trivia round, and EJAE's own rough demos paired with the finished songs. No merch, no unboxings, no sales pitches — just fans making things because they love the songs, and the people who actually made it. A pause-and-talk card from the Movie Companion is tucked into the fan-films section. Watch with Papai. (Fan-made videos linked to their creators on YouTube; all credit to the makers.)
